sections.h: Sirach 24: Wisdom pitches her tent in Israel
sections.b:
The central poem of Sirach lets Wisdom praise herself before the assembly of the Most High. She came out of God's mouth, lived in the heights with her throne in the pillar of cloud, and walked the sky and the deep. Looking for a place to rest among the nations, she was told by her Creator, "Pitch your tent in Jacob" (Sirach 24:8). She served in the holy tent, settled in Zion, grew like the land's best trees and smelled like the temple incense. Then Ben Sira names her: "All these things are the book of the covenant of God Most High, the law Moses commanded" (Sirach 24:23). Wisdom is the Torah. Baruch says the same (Baruch 4:1), and 1 Enoch tells the reverse story of a Wisdom who found no home (1 Enoch 42:1–2).

Christian readers have heard the poem of Christ, the wisdom of God who pitched his tent among us (John 1:14; 1 Corinthians 1:24), and Catholic liturgy has also read it of Mary. Ben Sira's own answer is the law.

common: In Sirach 24 Wisdom is identified with the law of Moses.
uncommon: Some readers take Sirach 24:28, "the first person did not finish knowing her", as a reference to Adam.

sections.b: Ben Sira ends Wisdom's song by saying that everything she has said of herself is "the book of the covenant of God Most High, the law Moses commanded, the heritage of the assemblies of Jacob" (Sirach 24:23). The last words quote the Greek of Deuteronomy 33:4: "Moses commanded us a law, the heritage of the assembly of Jacob" (Deuteronomy 33:4). The law then overflows with wisdom like the four rivers of Eden and the Jordan (Sirach 24:25–27), so deep that no student ever finishes it. This is one of the clearest early statements that God's wisdom and the Torah are one, an idea Paul answers when he calls Christ the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24) and when he speaks of the law as a guardian until Christ (Galatians 3:24).
sections.refs: Sirach 24:23–29; Deuteronomy 33:4; Deuteronomy 4:6; Baruch 4:1; Galatians 3:24; 1 Corinthians 1:24

sections.h: Wisdom from God's mouth and John's Word
sections.b: Wisdom says, "I came out of the Most High's mouth" (Sirach 24:3), and God tells her, "Pitch your tent in Jacob" (Sirach 24:8). John's prologue says the Word was with God in the beginning and "pitched his tent among us" (John 1:14), using the same tent verb without its prefix. Many scholars think John drew on this Jewish picture of Wisdom. The difference is as important as the likeness: for Ben Sira, Wisdom became the book of the law (Sirach 24:23); for John, the Word "became flesh".

sections.h: "The beginning of sin came from a woman" (Sirach 25:24)
sections.b: In the middle of a poem on the evil wife, Ben Sira writes, "The beginning of sin came from a woman, and on account of her we all die" (Sirach 25:24). The Hebrew of Cairo Genizah Manuscript C has the same: "from a woman is the beginning of guilt, and because of her we perish together". Most readers take the woman as Eve (Genesis 3:6). Others, following Jack Levison, read it of a bad wife who leads her husband into sin and an early death, since the poem is about wives and the next chapter says a good wife doubles a man's days. Read of Eve, the verse goes beyond Genesis, which holds both the man and the woman to account (Genesis 3:12–19), and differs from Paul, who says sin entered "through one man" (Romans 5:12). The Wisdom of Solomon gives yet another answer: death came "through the devil's envy" (Wisdom of Solomon 2:24).
sections.refs: Sirach 25:24; Genesis 3:6–19; Romans 5:12; 1 Timothy 2:13–14; Wisdom of Solomon 2:24

common: Sirach 25:24 is usually read as blaming Eve for the beginning of sin and death.
uncommon: Sirach 25:24 may speak of a bad wife and her husband, not of Eve and humanity.

claude.title: Ben Sira's own view of death
claude.body: Elsewhere Ben Sira treats death as the Lord's decree for all flesh (Sirach 41:3–4) and says the Lord made humans from earth and turned them back to it (Sirach 17:1). That fits the bad-wife reading of 25:24 better than a story of the fall. This is Claude's observation, not a checked published argument.

sections.h: The evil wife and the good wife (Sirach 25–26)
sections.b: Ben Sira gives young men two poems side by side. The evil wife is worse than a lion and a dragon (Sirach 25:16), a sandy climb for an old man (Sirach 25:20), and a husband who cannot guide her should "cut her away from your flesh" (Sirach 25:26), that is, divorce her, undoing the "one flesh" of Genesis 2:24. The good wife makes her husband happy and doubles his days (Sirach 26:1), and she is the Lord's gift to those who fear him (Sirach 26:3, 14), as beautiful in her home as the sun in the sky and the lamp in the temple (Sirach 26:16–17). The Talmud quotes the good-wife and bad-wife sayings in Ben Sira's name (Yevamot 63b; Sanhedrin 100b). Ben Sira's advice on divorce is more permissive than Jesus' answer, "What God has yoked together, then, no human being should separate" (Matthew 19:6).
sections.refs: Sirach 25:13–26:18; Genesis 2:24; Deuteronomy 24:1; Proverbs 18:22; Proverbs 21:9; Matthew 19:3–9

sections.b: Sirach 26:2 praises "a wife of strength" who cheers her husband, and the Hebrew of Manuscript C has the very phrase of Proverbs 31:10, eshet chayil. Sirach 28:15 uses the same Greek words for good wives whom slander has driven out of their homes. Ben Sira's picture is narrower than Proverbs 31, which praises a wife who buys fields and plants vineyards (Proverbs 31:16): he calls it shame when a wife supports her husband (Sirach 25:22).

sections.h: Tested by talk; the third tongue (Sirach 27–28)
sections.b: Ben Sira tests people by their speech: a sieve keeps the rubbish, a furnace proves the potter's jars, "so the words a man says show the thoughts of his heart" (Sirach 27:6), much as Jesus says the mouth speaks what overflows from the heart (Matthew 12:34). He warns against betraying secrets (Sirach 27:16–21) and the winker who flatters and then trips you up (Sirach 27:22–23). Chapter 28 adds the spark that one mouth can blow up or spit out (Sirach 28:12), and the long poem on "the tongue of a third party", slander, which has killed more than the sword (Sirach 28:13–23). The Talmud's saying that "third speech" kills three, speaker, hearer and victim, uses the same idiom (Arakhin 15b). James takes up the same pictures (James 3:5–10).

sections.h: Forgive, and your sins will be released (Sirach 28:1–7)
sections.b: Ben Sira teaches, "Forgive the wrong your neighbor did to you, and then, when you pray, your own sins will be released" (Sirach 28:2). A man who is "only flesh" and keeps up his anger cannot ask God for healing (Sirach 28:3–5). This is the closest saying before Jesus to the Lord's Prayer: "forgive us the debts we owe, just as we ourselves have forgiven the people who owe us" (Matthew 6:12; compare Mark 11:25). Jesus' parable of the unforgiving slave adds that God's mercy comes first (Matthew 18:23–35).

Ben Sira tells his students to be patient with the poor, to help them "because the commandment says so" (Sirach 29:9), and to lose money for a brother rather than let it rust under a rock. "Store up your treasure as the Most High commands" (Sirach 29:11): alms will rescue the giver and fight for him better than a shield (Sirach 29:12–13). Tobit says the same (Tobit 4:9–10), and Jesus speaks of treasure in heaven (Matthew 6:19–21). The Latin of 29:12 reads "in the heart of the poor". Whether such giving earns merit is the question of the "Where Christians differ" card at Tobit 4.
sections.refs: Sirach 29:8–13; Tobit 4:7–11; Tobit 12:8–9; Daniel 4:27; Matthew 6:19–21; Luke 12:33

sections.b: Lending to a neighbor in need is mercy and keeps the commandments (Sirach 29:1; Deuteronomy 15:7–11), and a borrower must repay on time (Sirach 29:2). But Ben Sira paints the borrower who kisses the lender's hand until he has the money, then makes excuses, pays back half or nothing, and turns the lender into an enemy (Sirach 29:4–7). On standing good for a neighbor's debt he is warmer than Proverbs (Proverbs 6:1–5; Proverbs 11:15): "A good man will stand good for his neighbor" (Sirach 29:14). Yet it has ruined many, so he ends, "Help your neighbor as far as you are able" (Sirach 29:20). Hebrews uses his word for a guarantor of Jesus (Hebrews 7:22).

sections.b: Ben Sira looks at hospitality from the guest's side. A man without a home of his own goes "from house to house" and cannot open his mouth (Sirach 29:24); he is made to pour the wine and set the table, then told, "Out you go, lodger; an honored guest is here" (Sirach 29:27). Better a poor roof of beams than splendid meals in strangers' homes (Sirach 29:22). The New Testament speaks to the host instead: "Do not forget to welcome strangers" (Hebrews 13:2), and Jesus tells guests to take the lowest place (Luke 14:7–11).

sections.h: Three, four and ten in Sirach 25–26
sections.b: Sirach 25–26 is full of counting sayings: three lovely things and three hateful people (Sirach 25:1–2), nine happy things and a tenth (Sirach 25:7–11), three fears and a fourth (Sirach 26:5–6), and two griefs and a third anger (Sirach 26:28). As in Proverbs 30, the last item often carries the point: the fear of the Lord above all (Sirach 25:11), a jealous rival wife (Sirach 26:6), a righteous man who goes back to sin (Sirach 26:28).

Ben Sira says the law fills with wisdom like the Pishon, the Tigris, the Euphrates and the Gihon, the four rivers of Eden (Genesis 2:10–14), with the Jordan added (Sirach 24:25–27). He then pictures his own teaching as a canal running into an orchard, the Greek paradeisos, the word the Greek Genesis uses for the garden of Eden (Sirach 24:30). In the Greek of 24:27 "like light" probably stands for the Hebrew "like the Nile", misread by one letter.

The Catechism says that "the Church's Tradition has often read the most beautiful texts on wisdom in relation to Mary", who is acclaimed in the liturgy as the "Seat of Wisdom" (Catechism 721). The Roman Missal of 1962 read the Latin of Sirach 24:14–16 (Greek 24:9–12) as the Epistle of a Mass of the Virgin Mary, Salve, sancta Parens. The Latin line "I am the mother of fair love" (Vulgate 24:24, Greek 24:18, Douay) became the title "Mother of Fair Love", under which Opus Dei keeps a feast on February 14. In Ben Sira's own poem the speaker is Wisdom.

Ben Sira gathers the Bible's pictures of wrongdoing that returns on the wrongdoer: a stone tossed straight up lands on your own head; "The one who digs a pit falls into it, and the one who sets a trap is caught in it" (Sirach 27:26); evil things roll back on the one who does them. The saying is Proverbs 26:27, with Ecclesiastes 10:8 and Psalm 7:15, and those who gloat over the fall of the godly are caught in the same way (Sirach 27:29).

Sirach 24 tells Wisdom's story with the tabernacle's words: she pitched her tent in the heights, her throne was in the pillar of cloud, God gave her tent a resting place, and she served in worship "in the holy tent" before settling in Zion (Sirach 24:4–10). Her fragrance is the holy incense of Exodus 30:34, "in the tent" (Sirach 24:15). The good wife of Sirach 26:16–18 is pictured with temple images too: the holy lampstand and gold on silver bases.
